node.label: Antoine Prost
node.date_label: Histoire de l’enseignement en France, 1800–1967 (1968) · Les Anciens Combattants et la société française: three-volume publication (1977) · Douze leçons sur l’histoire (1996)
node.description: A French historian of education, social life and the aftermath of war who also examines historical knowledge and practice. Maurice Agulhon’s substantive reading describes the veterans study as joining organization, social composition and commemorative practices, while challenging an automatic identification of veterans with fascism. Agulhon also questions whether that correction goes too far. Danièle Voldman reads Douze leçons as both a methodological exposition and a situated defence of historical understanding. These readings support the entry without claiming that the underlying books have been read in full.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Histoire de l’enseignement en France, 1800–1967 (1968); Les Anciens Combattants et la société française, 1914–1939 (three volumes, 1977; with collaboration of Philippe Billois); Douze leçons sur l’histoire (1996).
node.scope_note: New identity is the French historian of education and veterans, distinguished from other Prost authors by matching institutional and publication records. Argument claims use named substantive readers Agulhon and Voldman. Book bodies remain unread. Billois’s collaboration, the three-volume format, original publication years and separate shorter/late editions stay explicit. No generic university, political-affiliation or influence arrows.

incident_edges.evidence_note: Agulhon 1979, pp. 831–832, read: specifically discusses November 11 ceremonies, monuments and village sociability. His account of Prost’s political correction includes reservations about its extent. No uncritical consensus or whole-book reading.

incident_edges.relationship: Makes methods, question formation and the historian’s social position explicit problems of historical knowledge.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Voldman’s substantive 1996 review, pp. 174–175, attributes this methodological and epistemological argument to Douze leçons. The book itself remains unread; this is not an inferred connection from its title alone.

incident_edges.relationship: Corbin reports Prost’s criticism that his historical practice gives insufficient attention to history’s civic and social mission.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Explicitly Corbin’s own recollection in the 2006 Vacarme interview, not a newly located text by Prost. Corbin acknowledges that the description may be right and explains his resistance to lessons-of-history arguments. His later 2013 interview also recalls Prost’s contrast between civic mission and writing for pleasure. This is a specific disagreement between colleagues, not generalized hostility or rejection of the quality of Corbin’s research.

neighbor_nodes.description: Studies remembering, commemoration and forgetting through social relations, narratives, bodies and cultural forms. Recollection is evidence requiring interpretation; memory and history are connected in different, contested ways.

neighbor_nodes.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering
strands.focus: Family, religious and class contexts organize recollection; a collective framework is not proof of one identical group memory.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); English selections (1992)

strands.title: Sites of memory and historical reconstruction
strands.focus: Sites combine material, symbolic and functional dimensions, extending beyond monuments alone.

strands.title: Habit, bodies and ceremony
strands.focus: Remembering includes bodily competence, not only recalled propositions or pictures.

strands.title: Communication and cultural objectivation
strands.focus: Everyday recollection and durable cultural forms operate differently; Assmann revises rather than merely repeats Halbwachs.

strands.title: Media and uses of cultural memory
strands.focus: Writing, images and monuments organize what can be stored and recalled.

strands.title: Mourning and cultural continuities after war
strands.focus: Traditional and modern forms overlap in Great War mourning; this is not a template for every subsequent catastrophe.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

strands.title: Holocaust memorials and their contexts
strands.focus: Memorial forms and meanings vary across places and institutions.

strands.title: Popular practices of historical knowledge
strands.focus: Family research, images and reenactment make historical work visible outside professional writing.

strands.title: Life histories, gender and subjectivity
strands.focus: Fascist everyday life and feminist psychoanalytic inquiry are distinct routes into interpreted recollection.

strands.title: Archival authority, access and inscription
strands.focus: Combe’s inquiry into access supplies a named resource to Derrida. His account differentiates archives from spontaneous memory and examines institutional authority and technical inscription. From the archival profession, Schwartz and Cook called archives 'active sites where social power is negotiated' whose appraisal and access shape collective memory (2002, abstract); the wider readership is on the entry archival_turn.

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public memory
strands.focus: Hayden’s collaborative practice links historical interpretation to lived places.

strands.title: Traditions in contact and conflict
strands.focus: Halbwachs explains revisions of collective remembering through contact with other groups and their traditions; social frameworks are not an assurance of a unanimous or unchanging past.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925), final concluding subsection

strands.title: Memorial production and public disagreement
strands.focus: Young’s Saarbrücken account follows a covert art project into public controversy and political recognition. His interpretation makes the memorial’s production and reception part of its meaning.
strands.works: Germany’s vanishing Holocaust monuments (1994), adapted extract

strands.title: Argentina: rights, remembrance and generations
strands.focus: Jelin examines competing public memories and tensions within human-rights activism. Her conclusion questions both political forgetting and repetition that prevents younger generations from reinterpreting the past.
strands.works: The Politics of Memory (1994), selected sections

strands.title: Vichy’s afterlife and historical inquiry
strands.focus: Rousso distinguishes memory as an object of research, as a preliminary examination of inherited representations, and as a way to extend an event’s historical study into its aftermath.
strands.works: Pour une histoire de la mémoire collective (1991), 163–166

strands.title: Jewish remembrance and historiography
strands.focus: Yerushalmi’s prologue asks why concern with historical meaning and remembrance need not give professional historical writing the central role. This is a situated historical question, not a timeless definition of Jewish people.

strands.title: Resources for studying forgetting
strands.focus: Jelin’s 1994 analysis explicitly draws on Yerushalmi’s transmission argument and Loraux’s treatment of amnesty and mourning. Their Spanish 1989 essays are distinct from Zakhor.
strands.works: Usos del olvido essays (1989), as used by Jelin (1994)

neighbor_nodes.label: Explanation & objectivity debates
neighbor_nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967
neighbor_nodes.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Analytic philosophy’s covering-law debate overlaps with historians’ arguments about evidence and interpretation without being identical to them. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.
neighbor_nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Becker’s 1931 address (published 1932); Hempel, “The Function of General Laws in History” (1942); Dray, Laws and Explanation in History (1957); Carr, What Is History? (1961); Elton, The Practice of History (1967).

representative_people.works: Augustine of Hippo (1967; new edition with epilogue 2000); The World of Late Antiquity (1971); The Cult of the Saints (1981); The Body and Society (1988; twentieth-anniversary introduction 2008); Journeys of the Mind (2023); “Augustine’s Friendship for Freedom” (interview conducted July 2026, published September 2026).

neighbor_nodes.scope_note: Covering laws, understanding action, historical facts, and objectivity are different disputes; participants do not form a shared school. Hempel’s probabilistic sketches, Dray’s challenge, Carr’s reciprocal research and Mink’s comprehension are distinct. Primary readings and publisher-only contexts are explicitly separated.

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s critique asks both how moral judgments arise and what they are worth; Rée and Schopenhauer are distinct interlocutors. Origin and later function must not be conflated.

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement
strands.focus: Barthes analyzes the presentation of reality; Bann uses that analysis while questioning its scope and preserving source-based scrutiny. Formal analysis alone does not decide a historical claim’s truth.

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture
strands.focus: Michelet’s account of reciprocal formation and Huizinga’s warning about surviving art raise different questions about historical knowledge; they do not deny the need for evidence.

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.

strands.title: Language use and following rules
strands.focus: Wittgenstein examines varied activities and similarities rather than one essence of language. Following a rule involves a practice; an interpretation cannot supply its own application without limit.

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment
strands.focus: Ryle distinguishes competent action from both an automatic movement and a performance governed by an endless series of prior theoretical decisions. A richer action description identifies purpose and circumstances.
strands.works: The Concept of Mind, II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts

strands.title: Narrative and historical understanding
strands.focus: White identifies particular philosophical interlocutors rather than responding to one undifferentiated philosophy of history.

strands.title: Laws, probability and explanation sketches
strands.focus: Hempel’s demand for testable relations permits incomplete research proposals and probabilistic accounts.

strands.title: Action and the limits of one explanatory model
strands.focus: Dray’s challenge includes reasons, uniqueness and pragmatic questions; it is not a ban on all generalization.
strands.works: Laws and Explanation (1957); Nature of Historical Explanation (1952)

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation
strands.focus: Becker and Carr preserve evidence while disputing self-interpreting facts; they do not offer identical positions.

strands.title: Historical craft, imagination and instruction
strands.focus: Elton’s research/writing/teaching agenda and Skinner’s apprenticeship reading identify practices of training.

strands.title: Narrative comprehension and truth
strands.focus: Mink separates grasping relations from truth tests and disputes both Gallie’s following and Hardy’s lived-narrative account.

strands.title: Knowledge of the past and speculative historical systems
strands.focus: Walsh’s scope distinguishes questions about inquiry from philosophies of the whole historical process.
